title: South Africa Financial Update | Key Market & Economic Developments | 23 July 2026
summary: SARB holds the repo rate at 7.00% in a 4-2 vote as 2026 GDP growth is forecast at 1.2%, while ARM unveils a R16bn capex plan, Pepkor eyes a R21.3bn fintech spin-off, and Mozambique's looming 2028 gas cliff threatens industrial energy costs.
body:
The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) has kept the repo rate unchanged at 7.00%, leaving the prime lending rate at 10.50%. The Monetary Policy Committee's decision was split 4–2, with four members opting to hold rates steady while two supported a 25-basis-point increase. Although headline inflation edged up to 5.0% in June, driven by fuel price volatility and persistent services inflation, easing global oil prices and a resilient rand provided enough support for the Bank to pause further tightening. Economic growth expectations remain modest, with GDP forecast at around 1.2% for 2026, reflecting high operating costs and subdued consumer and business confidence.

On the corporate front, African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) came under pressure after unveiling a nearly R16 billion capital investment plan focused on expanding its mining operations. Pepkor announced a significant R21.3 billion fintech expansion strategy, with long-term ambitions of listing the business separately as it strengthens its presence in South Africa's informal economy. Meanwhile, Absa is nearing a strategic transaction in Tanzania that would consolidate approximately R49.2 billion in regional banking assets. In retail, Mr Price reported encouraging quarterly sales growth, supported by continued strong demand across its NKD business.

Attention is also turning to longer-term structural challenges. Industry stakeholders continue to warn about South Africa's looming 2028 gas cliff, as natural gas supplies from Mozambique's Pande and Temane fields are expected to decline significantly after 2028. Without accelerated investment in LNG infrastructure, many industrial users could face energy costs between two and five times higher if forced to switch to LPG or diesel alternatives. At the same time, the technology sector is responding to a recent cyberattack that prompted Mustek and Rectron to launch forensic recovery efforts, while Treasury continues to defend funding freezes affecting 69 financially distressed municipalities, highlighting ongoing concerns over municipal finances and their impact on the broader business environment.

title: South Africa Financial Update | Key Market & Economic Developments | 24 July 2026
summary: SARB surprises markets by holding the repo rate at 7.00% in a 4-2 vote despite hotter June inflation, lifts 2026 GDP forecast to 1.4%, while transport inflation spikes 12.7% and municipalities weigh solar grid-access fees.
body:
The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) surprised markets by keeping the repo rate unchanged at 7.00%, leaving the prime lending rate at 10.50%. Governor Lesetja Kganyago said the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted 4–2 in favour of holding rates steady. Most economists had expected a 25-basis-point increase after June's higher-than-anticipated inflation reading.

The decision reflects a balancing act between rising inflation risks and a still-fragile economy. While higher global oil prices, fuelled by supply disruptions in the Middle East, have pushed transport costs higher, broader consumer and services inflation has remained relatively contained. The SARB also lifted its 2026 economic growth forecast to 1.4%, up from 1.2%, although it cautioned that economic activity is likely to remain subdued during the second and third quarters as consumer and business confidence stays under pressure.

June's headline consumer inflation accelerated to 5.0% year-on-year, largely driven by a 12.7% increase in transport inflation following earlier fuel price hikes. Looking ahead, preliminary figures from the Central Energy Fund (CEF) suggest motorists could see a modest petrol price cut of around 50 cents per litre in August. Diesel users, however, may face increases of between 60 and 90 cents per litre as global supply constraints continue to influence oil markets. Elevated energy prices and ongoing supply chain disruptions remain the biggest inflation risks for the months ahead.

In the business sector, Business Leadership South Africa (BLSA) has warned that the pace of structural reform is beginning to slow. The organisation stressed that improvements to transport infrastructure and local government performance are essential if South Africa is to achieve stronger and more sustainable economic growth.

Meanwhile, a growing number of financially distressed municipalities are considering introducing fixed grid-access charges for households with solar installations. The move is aimed at recovering declining electricity revenue as more consumers reduce their dependence on the national grid.

Financial markets remain relatively stable, with the rand trading in the region of R16.50 to R16.60 against the US dollar. Despite persistent inflationary pressures, the SARB's decision to leave interest rates unchanged signals confidence that inflation can be managed while continuing to support a modest economic recovery.

title: South African Business & Financial Update | 24 July 2026
summary: SARB weighs mandatory PayShap adoption for banks as instant payments lag global peers, its rate hold draws praise from property and agriculture sectors, Home Affairs launches Phase II of the Trusted Employer Scheme for fintech talent, and the dtic wraps its Essential Oils Conference in Pretoria.
body:
South Africa's economic landscape continues to evolve as policymakers, businesses, and industry leaders focus on reforms aimed at supporting long-term growth and improving competitiveness.

The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) is considering making participation in the PayShap fast-payment system mandatory for commercial banks. Three years after its launch, PayShap processes around 60 million transactions per month—equivalent to roughly one transaction per person each month, well below adoption levels seen in countries such as Brazil. According to SARB executive Pradeep Maharaj, wider use of instant digital payments could reduce reliance on cash and potentially add up to one percentage point to South Africa's GDP growth over time.

The Reserve Bank's decision to keep the repo rate at 7.00% and the prime lending rate at 10.50% has been broadly welcomed across several sectors. Property market analysts from Standard Bank Home Services and the ooba Group said stable interest rates provide much-needed certainty for homebuyers by keeping monthly repayments predictable, particularly in the first-time buyer and affordable housing markets. The agricultural sector also welcomed the pause in borrowing costs, although farmers continue to face pressure from higher diesel and fertiliser prices linked to ongoing global supply constraints. Economists at PSG Financial Services noted that the Monetary Policy Committee adopted a more measured tone than many had anticipated, choosing to monitor Middle East energy risks rather than immediately factoring them into its central economic outlook.

Meanwhile, the Department of Home Affairs has officially launched Phase II of the expanded Trusted Employer Scheme (TES). The latest phase introduces dedicated visa pathways designed to attract international financial, fintech, and technical professionals to South Africa's emerging Synthetic Financial Centre (SFC). The initiative is expected to significantly reduce visa processing times, helping strengthen the country's competitiveness as a destination for highly skilled talent.

On the trade front, the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (the dtic) is wrapping up its Essential Oils Conference in Pretoria, held from 23 to 24 July. The conference forms part of a broader strategy to help local producers move beyond exporting raw natural resources and expand into higher-value manufacturing for the global cosmetics, wellness, and essential oils market, which is valued at more than US$15 billion.

title: South African Corporate & Market Update | 24 July 2026
summary: Deputy Finance Minister David Masondo resigns as PIC board chair amid governance tensions, Pepkor unveils a R21.3bn fintech spin-off plan, ARM commits R16bn to mine modernisation and solar capacity, industry warns on the 2028 gas cliff, and Mustek/Rectron continue cyberattack recovery.
body:
Several major corporate and institutional developments are shaping South Africa's business landscape, with leadership changes, strategic investments, and infrastructure challenges remaining firmly in focus.

Deputy Finance Minister David Masondo has officially stepped down as Chairperson of the Public Investment Corporation (PIC) board. His resignation follows weeks of reported governance tensions at the state-owned asset manager, which oversees more than R2.6 trillion in assets on behalf of public sector pension funds. Masondo said the decision was taken in the interests of stability and public confidence, underscoring the importance of strong leadership at Africa's largest asset manager for both investors and the broader financial markets.

Retail group Pepkor has announced a major restructuring that will establish a dedicated R21.3 billion fintech business, with long-term plans that could include a separate stock market listing. The strategy reflects Pepkor's continued expansion beyond discount retail into digital financial services, including micro-lending, digital payments, and insurance products aimed at South Africa's informal and lower-income markets.

Mining company African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) also drew investor attention after outlining an ambitious R16 billion capital investment programme. The planned expenditure will focus on modernising deep-level mining operations, expanding renewable energy capacity through solar generation, and strengthening logistics to reduce the impact of ongoing rail infrastructure constraints.

Energy experts and industry groups have renewed warnings about South Africa's looming "gas cliff", expected around 2028, as natural gas supplies from Sasol's mature Mozambican fields begin to decline. The anticipated shortfall could place significant pressure on manufacturing hubs in Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal, increasing the urgency for government and the private sector to accelerate investment in liquefied natural gas (LNG) import infrastructure and alternative energy solutions.

Meanwhile, JSE-listed ICT distributor Mustek and its subsidiary Rectron are continuing recovery efforts following a significant cyberattack that disrupted parts of their internal operational networks. Both companies have launched forensic investigations to determine the cause and extent of the incident while working to restore affected systems and strengthen cybersecurity measures.

title: South African Infrastructure, Trade & Market Update | 24 July 2026
summary: Durban's DCT Pier 2 posts an 18% improvement in vessel turnaround as freight rail bottlenecks persist, Valterra Platinum forecasts earnings up more than 1,300% on a PGM price surge, AGOA renewal talks intensify for SA exporters, and SARB models a $100/barrel oil scenario that could delay its inflation target to mid-2027.
body:
South Africa's economic outlook continues to be shaped by improvements in logistics, stronger commodity markets, evolving trade discussions, and ongoing global energy risks.

Transnet's efforts to introduce greater private-sector participation are beginning to show encouraging results at the Durban Container Terminal (DCT) Pier 2. Average vessel turnaround times have improved by approximately 18% month-on-month, providing early signs that congestion at one of the country's busiest ports is easing. While progress at the ports is welcome, freight rail remains a significant challenge. Bulk export corridors, particularly those transporting coal and iron ore, continue to experience bottlenecks that are limiting mining exports and weighing on industry revenues.

South Africa's platinum group metal (PGM) producers are benefiting from a sharp recovery in global commodity prices. Valterra Platinum has issued a strong trading update, forecasting headline earnings to increase by more than 1,300%, to between R18.5 billion and R22.2 billion. The turnaround has been driven by an 85% rise in the US dollar PGM basket price, combined with improved operational performance following maintenance disruptions experienced during 2025.

Trade officials are also closely monitoring discussions in Washington over the future of the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). South Africa's automotive, agricultural, and wine industries rely heavily on the agreement's duty-free access to the US market. With the current framework approaching its renewal deadline, government trade representatives are advocating for an early extension to provide certainty for exporters and avoid disruptions to manufacturing and export planning for 2027.

Following its decision to leave interest rates unchanged, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) also outlined the economic scenarios underpinning its latest forecasts. The Bank's baseline outlook assumes oil prices remain close to current levels, allowing inflation to gradually return towards its 3% target over the medium term. However, it also modelled a more adverse scenario in which crude oil prices rise to US$100 per barrel throughout 2026 as a result of escalating tensions in the Middle East. In that case, higher fuel costs could keep inflation above the Reserve Bank's target until at least mid-2027, potentially requiring further interest rate increases to contain price pressures.

title: South Africa's Key Financial and Business Developments | 12 August 2026
summary: Nedbank data shows announced fixed investment plunging 81% to a post-2017 low of R137.7bn, unemployment rises to 33.6% as the formal sector sheds 41,000 jobs, the rand holds near a five-month high around R16.19/USD, and Shoprite and Boxer post strong retail growth.
body:
South Africa's investment climate remained under pressure on 12 August 2026, with new data pointing to a sharp decline in announced fixed investment, persistent labour-market challenges and continued caution among businesses. At the same time, the rand remained relatively resilient, while retailers and small businesses continued to adapt to changing economic conditions.

Nedbank's H1 2026 Capital Expenditure Project Listing showed that announced fixed investment projects fell by 81%, or about R580 billion, compared with 2025. Total commitments stood at R137.7 billion, the lowest level recorded since 2017. The private sector accounted for R107 billion of the planned investment, with renewable energy projects making up a significant share. These included the final tranche of REIPPP Bid Window 7, as well as the Notsi and Orkney solar PV projects. Nedbank expects Gross Fixed Capital Formation to grow by only 0.6% in 2026, reflecting continued caution from businesses amid global economic risks.

The rand, meanwhile, remained firm near a five-month high at around R16.19 to the US dollar. Its recent strength has been supported by softer US labour-market data, which has reduced expectations for US interest-rate increases and improved sentiment towards risk-sensitive emerging-market currencies. South African government bonds were slightly weaker, with benchmark 2035 yields rising to between 8.41% and 8.42%. Gold was trading at about $4,401.10 an ounce, while Brent crude was around $89.45 a barrel.

The labour market also came under renewed pressure. Official Statistics South Africa data showed that unemployment increased to 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, up from 32.7% in the first quarter. The formal sector lost roughly 41,000 jobs during the quarter, although the informal economy provided some relief by adding about 34,000 jobs. Informal employment reached approximately 3.57 million people, underscoring the growing importance of the informal economy as a source of income and economic resilience. Estimates suggest that the broader unrecorded value of informal economic activity could be close to R1 trillion.

In the retail sector, competition is increasingly shifting away from simply opening more traditional stores towards building broader consumer ecosystems. Shoprite added 262 stores over the past year and continued expanding into non-grocery categories through businesses such as Petshop Science and Uniq Clothing. Boxer also reported strong momentum, recording 12.3% sales growth for its 2026 financial year and increasing its store network to 576 outlets.

MTN, meanwhile, warned investors of profit pressure as it faced operational and macroeconomic challenges across its international operations, with conditions in Iran having a particularly significant impact. The telecommunications group's trading statement highlighted the continued difficulty of operating across complex and volatile international markets.

Small-business support also came under scrutiny in Parliament. The Portfolio Committee on Small Business Development questioned the Small Enterprise Development Finance Agency (SEDFA) over the R500 million Spaza Shop Support Fund. The fund has faced criticism following findings by the Public Protector concerning irregularities in the way financial assistance was disbursed.

Overall, the latest developments paint a mixed picture of the South African economy. While the rand and parts of the retail sector are showing resilience, the sharp fall in announced investment and rising unemployment point to continued weaknesses in the broader economy. The resilience of the informal sector and the ongoing expansion of renewable energy and retail businesses provide some positives, but stronger investment and job creation will remain critical to improving South Africa's growth prospects.

title: South African Market and Economic Overview | 27 July 2026
summary: JSE closes the week flat at 109,398.10 as basic materials gain 5.28% and tech falls 5.28%, SARB holds the repo rate at 7.0% despite inflation rising to 5.0%, retail sales grow 2.3%, and Treasury moves to remove nine PIC non-executive directors.
body:
South African markets ended the week relatively flat, with the JSE All Share Index closing at 109,398.10, down 0.15%. The basic materials sector was the standout performer, gaining 5.28%, while the technology sector fell by a similar 5.28%, highlighting the contrasting performance across key sectors.

The South African Reserve Bank kept the repo rate unchanged at 7.0%, despite consumer inflation increasing from 4.5% in May to 5.0% in June. The rise in inflation was largely driven by higher transport, fuel and utility costs, reinforcing the SARB's cautious approach as it balances inflationary pressures against economic growth.

Consumer activity showed some resilience, with retail sales increasing by 2.3% in May. However, this positive performance continues to be weighed down by structural challenges. Ongoing inefficiencies at South Africa's borders are reportedly costing the economy as much as R16 billion a year, adding further pressure to trade and economic activity.

On the corporate governance front, National Treasury held a general meeting on 27 July to address the proposed removal of nine non-executive directors from the Public Investment Corporation board. The developments follow a period of heightened scrutiny around governance at the PIC, including the earlier precautionary suspension of CEO Patrick Dlamini.

Global markets also continued to influence South African assets. Brent crude traded close to $100 a barrel before easing as tensions surrounding the US-Iran situation temporarily subsided. At the same time, gold prices moved higher as investors sought the relative safety of precious metals amid wider concerns about global trade and geopolitical risks.

Overall, the week reflected a mixed environment for South African markets, with resilient consumer activity and strong performance from basic materials offset by inflationary pressures, weaker technology shares, governance concerns and continued exposure to global commodity and geopolitical developments.

title: Market, Currency & Economic Update | 27 August 2026
summary: The rand steadies near R15.95–R15.96/USD as JSE precious metals stocks head for their best month in two decades on a gold rally past $4,600/oz, Harmony Gold posts 87% earnings growth, Sanlam flags a mixed H1, and producer inflation eases to around 6.1%.
body:
The South African rand has remained relatively stable, trading around R15.95–R15.96 against the US dollar as markets digest the latest July economic data and look for further guidance from global central bank meetings and policy discussions.

Precious metals and mining shares have been a major highlight, with JSE-listed counters heading towards their strongest monthly performance in two decades. The rally has been driven largely by robust gold prices, with the FTSE/JSE Precious Metals and Mining Index gaining roughly 38% so far this month. Spot gold has also remained elevated, trading around $4,610–$4,625 per ounce, providing strong support for gold-focused producers.

Corporate earnings have added to the positive momentum. Harmony Gold reported an impressive 87% increase in annual headline earnings per share to R43.63 for the financial year ended 30 June 2026. The strong performance was supported by a 35% increase in the average gold price, as well as the contribution from its newly acquired Australian copper asset. The company also announced a record total dividend payout of 750 cents per share.

Sanlam has also provided an update on its performance for the six months to June 2026. The group expects earnings per share to increase by as much as 34%, helped by a once-off gain from the disposal of its active asset management business to Ninety One. However, headline earnings per share are expected to decline by up to 20%, reflecting weaker shareholder investment returns compared with the same period last year.

On the economic front, Statistics South Africa released the latest Producer Price Index figures for July, with market expectations pointing to an annual increase of around 6.1%, down from 7.5% in June. The continued moderation in producer inflation provides some relief, although broader economic conditions remain challenging.

Growth momentum also appears to have cooled during the second quarter. While real net consumer salaries showed a modest improvement in July as headline inflation eased, other indicators continue to point to underlying weakness. Mining production, for example, declined by 5.4% year-on-year in May, while manufacturing activity has also remained under pressure.

Overall, South African markets are benefiting from strong precious-metal prices and encouraging performances from parts of the mining sector, while the broader economy continues to face slower growth and persistent pressure across key productive industries.

title: Markets, Corporate & Economic Update | 27 August 2026
summary: The rand holds near six-month highs around R15.95–R15.96/USD as the JSE All Share stays flat and gold miners rally on spot prices near $4,625/oz; Harmony Gold posts record profits, MTN weighs investors for its IHS Nigeria stake, and the IDC reports a R5.6bn loss after Foskor accounting errors.
body:
The South African rand remained steady at around R15.95–R15.96 against the US dollar, trading close to six-month highs. Overall market sentiment was relatively calm as local investors assessed the latest Producer Price Index data while keeping a close eye on signals from the US Federal Reserve’s Jackson Hole symposium for clues on the future direction of interest rates.

On the JSE, the All Share Index was virtually unchanged, slipping just 0.01%. Precious-metal mining shares, however, continued their remarkable rally and are on track for some of their strongest monthly gains in decades. Gold remained firmly supported, with spot prices trading around $4,625 per ounce as investors continued to seek safe-haven assets and position for potential global interest-rate cuts.

Corporate activity remained active. Harmony Gold benefited from record gold prices, reporting a substantial increase in full-year profits, although the company continued to face losses linked to its hedging positions.

MTN Group was also in focus amid reports that it is considering strategic investors for its R17.5 billion stake in tower operator IHS Nigeria. In a separate development, MTN has partnered with UAE businessman Al Ashram on plans to develop artificial-intelligence data centres across Africa, highlighting the growing investment opportunity around the continent’s digital infrastructure.

The Industrial Development Corporation reported a significant R5.6 billion loss and restated previous financial results following accounting errors at Foskor, alongside continued impairments related to mining rights. Meanwhile, the Competition Commission approved Emira Property Fund’s sale of Randridge Mall in Gauteng to Goat Wholesale.

PPC also provided some continuity at executive level, formally extending the contract of CEO through to 2030. OUTsurance, meanwhile, indicated a strong improvement in its headline performance, supported by better local underwriting conditions in South Africa.

On the economic front, BankservAfrica data showed a modest improvement in real net salaries in July, marking the first increase in nine months. The improvement offers some relief to households as easing headline inflation begins to provide slightly more breathing room for consumers.

The aviation sector is facing a different set of pressures, with supply constraints affecting Johannesburg’s jet-fuel pipeline following a shutdown at Sasol’s Natref refinery. Airlines have consequently been required to manage their fuel supplies more carefully to minimise disruptions.

On the international trade front, pressure from US tariffs is encouraging South Africa and Brazil to strengthen their industrial and trade cooperation within the broader BRICS framework. The move reflects growing efforts among emerging-market economies to deepen trade relationships and reduce their exposure to shifting global trade policies.

Overall, the South African market remains supported by strong precious-metal prices and improving conditions in selected sectors, while investors continue to balance these positives against domestic economic pressures, energy constraints and an uncertain global policy environment.

title: South African Market Update | 28 August 2026
summary: SARB's leading business cycle indicator falls 1.6% q/q as mining output drops 5.4% and manufacturing 4.3%, the rand holds near R15.95/USD ahead of Jackson Hole, business liquidations ease 4.9% year-to-date, Discovery forecasts up to 36% earnings growth, and Truworths shares slide on weaker profits.
body:
South Africa’s economy is showing signs of losing momentum after a relatively strong start to the year. Following GDP growth of 0.5% in the first quarter, the South African Reserve Bank’s composite leading business cycle indicator declined by 1.6% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter, pointing to growing pressure on economic activity. Recent data from Stats SA also highlighted weakness across key sectors, with mining production contracting by 5.4% year-on-year, driven largely by declines in iron ore, coal and platinum-group metals (PGMs), while manufacturing output fell by 4.3%. The official second-quarter GDP figures are due to be released on 8 September and will provide a clearer picture of the economy’s underlying performance.

In financial markets, the rand was trading near R15.95 to the US dollar as investors weighed the latest inflation data and awaited further signals from global central banks at the Jackson Hole symposium. Producer price inflation for July eased to around 6.1%, offering some relief on the inflation front. Meanwhile, benchmark South African government bond yields remained relatively steady, with the 2035 bond trading around 8.44%.

Business liquidations have also continued to reflect pressure on parts of the economy. A total of 1,601 business liquidations were recorded during the year to date in 2026, representing a 4.9% decline compared with the same period in 2025. Despite the overall improvement, the Financial, Insurance and Real Estate sectors remain particularly vulnerable, accounting for 226 liquidations so far this year.

On the corporate front, Discovery delivered an encouraging trading update, forecasting headline earnings per share growth of between 31% and 36% for the financial year ended 30 June 2026. Normalised profit is expected to increase by 15% to 20%, supported by solid performances from Discovery South Africa and Vitality Global, as well as lower finance costs following a reduction in debt. One of the key developments was Discovery Bank reaching profitability for the first time, recording a profit of R75 million at the half-year stage. Investors will be watching closely for the group’s full-year results, which are scheduled for release on 3 September.

Truworths International, however, faced a more challenging market reaction. Its shares fell by more than 4% following the release of its full-year results. Headline earnings per share declined by 2.65% to 732.2 cents, while group profit fell by 4.7% to R2.66 billion. Weak consumer disposable income in South Africa weighed on active credit account usage in the African division, while the stronger rand reduced the reported contribution from its UK-based Office business.

In the banking and capital markets space, Standard Bank has finalised the redemption mechanics for its RLN026 Equity Linked Notes, which mature on 2 September 2026. Noteholders have until midday on 28 August to elect physical delivery of the underlying ETF. Those who do not make an election will default to cash redemption at 134,000 cents per note. The notes are expected to be formally delisted on 3 September.

Overall, the South African market is entering a period of mixed signals. Slower economic activity and pressure on consumers remain key concerns, while easing inflation, a relatively stable rand and improving corporate earnings in selected sectors provide some support. With the release of second-quarter GDP figures and several major corporate results approaching, investors will be watching closely for signs of whether the recent economic weakness is temporary or indicative of a broader slowdown.

title: South African Financial & Business Update | 28 August 2026
summary: Truworths reports softer FY2026 results as retail sales dip 0.9%, Discovery forecasts up to 36% earnings growth, the V&A Waterfront unveils a R1.4bn retiree residential project, IDC auditors flag around R2bn in reporting errors, and vehicle buyers shift toward more affordable models below R500,000.
body:
South Africa’s corporate and economic landscape remains mixed, with several companies reporting contrasting performances while businesses and households continue to face pressure from elevated living costs and a challenging economic environment.

Truworths is among the retailers feeling the squeeze from weaker consumer spending. The company reported a softer set of full-year results for FY2026, with retail sales declining by 0.9% to R21.8 billion and headline earnings per share falling by 2.65%. Truworths pointed to continued pressure on credit-dependent South African consumers, while the stronger rand also weighed on the contribution from its UK-based Office business.

By contrast, Discovery delivered a more positive outlook, forecasting headline earnings per share growth of between 31% and 36% for FY2026. The expected improvement reflects strong performance across its core operations, with Discovery Bank also reaching profitability for the first time, marking an important milestone for the group.

The V&A Waterfront is also expanding its residential offering, announcing a R1.4 billion development aimed specifically at retirees. The project adds to the precinct’s growing residential footprint and reflects continued demand for lifestyle-focused developments in established urban locations.

Governance and financial reporting remain areas of concern at the Industrial Development Corporation. Auditors have flagged approximately R2 billion in financial reporting errors, raising questions around the quality of financial controls and reporting at one of South Africa’s key development-finance institutions.

At the broader business level, financial stress remains evident despite some improvement in overall liquidation numbers. More than 1,600 businesses have been liquidated in South Africa so far in 2026. While business liquidations fell by 23.2% year-on-year in July, individual and business insolvencies increased sharply between June and July, highlighting the continued financial strain facing parts of the economy.

Economic momentum has also moderated following a relatively solid start to the year. Second-quarter indicators point to softer activity as households continue to grapple with persistent costs, limiting disposable income and weighing on consumer spending. The pressure is particularly visible in sectors that depend heavily on household consumption and credit.

The vehicle-finance market is reflecting these changing consumer dynamics, with buyers increasingly gravitating towards more affordable vehicles priced below R500,000. The shift suggests that households are becoming more cautious about taking on larger financial commitments and are prioritising affordability as financing costs and other household expenses remain elevated.

The energy sector remains another important area of focus. Eskom continues to face pressure from fuel-supply and infrastructure constraints, while the temporary shutdown of Sasol’s refinery operations has added to concerns around jet-fuel supply. Energy Minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa has highlighted the need for greater private-sector participation and investment in energy infrastructure and generation capacity. The government is also weighing measures aimed at protecting consumers and managing the impact of higher energy costs, while navigating fiscal pressures and the country’s elevated debt burden.

Overall, South Africa’s economic picture remains one of cautious resilience. Stronger corporate performances from some businesses are being offset by weaker consumer demand, financial stress among smaller enterprises and continued challenges in the energy sector. The direction of household spending, business confidence and policy measures around energy and investment will remain important factors for markets and the broader economy in the months ahead.

title: South African Markets Steady as Inflation Cools, Debt Costs Rise and Global Investors Watch the Fed | 28 August 2026
summary: The rand holds near R16.00/USD as JSE trading stays subdued, producer inflation slows sharply to 5.7%, government debt-servicing costs hit R432.4bn a year on R6.33 trillion of debt, the IDC plans its first private shareholding in 86 years, and markets await Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole address.
body:
South African financial markets are taking a cautious approach on Friday, 28 August 2026, with the rand holding firm near some of its strongest levels of the year despite continued strength in the US dollar globally.

The rand is trading at around R16.00 to the US dollar, R18.63 to the euro and R21.74 to the British pound. Recent inflation data has provided some support for the currency, although global market movements and expectations around US interest rates remain key drivers.

On the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, trading opened relatively subdued, with the All Share Index slipping 0.01% and the Top 40 Index falling 0.15%. The benchmark 2035 South African government bond yield, meanwhile, edged 1.5 basis points higher to 8.47%.

Commodity markets are also in focus. Gold is trading at around $4,584 an ounce as investors await further signals on global monetary policy. Brent crude has moved higher to between $88.35 and $89.31 a barrel, with ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continuing to influence oil prices.

South Africa's latest producer inflation figures offered some encouragement. Producer Price Index inflation slowed sharply to 5.7% year-on-year in July, down from 7.5% in June and below the market consensus of 6.1%. While the slowdown suggests some easing in price pressures, economists continue to warn that energy costs, imported inflation and volatile global oil prices could create upside risks in the months ahead.

The country's growing debt burden remains a major concern. National Treasury figures show that South Africa is spending approximately R1.18 billion every day — or R432.4 billion a year — simply servicing its gross government debt. Total government debt has reached around R6.33 trillion, equivalent to roughly 77.3% of GDP, highlighting the increasing pressure that debt-service costs are placing on the country's finances.

In the corporate sector, the Industrial Development Corporation has announced plans to introduce private shareholding for the first time in its 86-year history. The move is aimed at unlocking additional funding to support industrial development and could represent a significant change in the way the state-owned development finance institution raises capital.

South Africa's aviation sector is also dealing with disruption following an unplanned outage at Sasol's Natref refinery, which has affected jet-fuel supplies to OR Tambo International Airport. Major airlines have responded by putting fuel-contingency measures in place as the industry works to manage the disruption.

Meanwhile, Johannesburg's retail landscape is expanding with the opening of the new R400 million Fleurhof Mall in the west of the city. The approximately 20,000-square-metre shopping centre officially opened its doors today, adding another major retail destination to one of Johannesburg's rapidly developing areas.

Internationally, investors are focused on the US Federal Reserve and the direction of interest rates. Markets are closely watching Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's upcoming address at the Jackson Hole symposium, where any indication of the Fed's thinking on inflation, economic growth and future rate cuts could have a significant impact on global markets, currencies and bond yields.

The technology sector is showing a sharp divergence. Nvidia shares jumped 8.7% after the chipmaker delivered strong long-term revenue guidance, reinforcing investor optimism around the continued expansion of artificial intelligence. Alphabet, however, is facing greater scrutiny, with its shares down more than 15% from their May peak as investors weigh the enormous costs of building AI infrastructure against the potential returns.

summary: Northam Platinum shares jump as much as 11% after an unsolicited takeover approach, miners accelerate the shift to renewable power at 20–30% below Eskom tariffs, Ramaphosa launches Phase 3 of the Government-Business Partnership targeting R50bn in mining capex by 2028, and Thungela sustains coal export volumes via improved rail access.
body:
South Africa’s mining and resources sector is entering a period of significant change, with potential corporate deals, the rapid shift towards renewable energy, government efforts to unlock investment and ongoing improvements in export logistics shaping the industry’s outlook.

Northam Platinum has emerged as a potential takeover target after disclosing that it had received an unsolicited, exploratory and non-binding approach from a major producer. The news sent Northam’s shares sharply higher on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, with the stock gaining as much as 11% following the announcement. The company has appointed financial and legal advisers and plans to assess any proposals from interested parties against the value and prospects of remaining an independent producer. The development could potentially reshape the competitive landscape of South Africa’s platinum group metals industry.

At the same time, Northam is continuing to push ahead with its renewable-energy strategy at its Eland PGM operations. The company is targeting a transition towards 100% renewable power offtake, part of a broader effort to reduce carbon emissions while limiting its exposure to Eskom’s electricity grid and rising power costs.

Renewable energy is becoming increasingly important across the wider mining industry. Companies such as Exxaro through Cennergi, Kumba Iron Ore, Sibanye-Stillwater and Anglo American are accelerating investments in private solar and wind power and entering into long-term renewable energy supply agreements. With private power purchase contracts currently estimated to be around 20% to 30% cheaper than standard Eskom grid tariffs, miners are gaining an opportunity to reduce electricity costs while protecting operating margins. The move is particularly significant for energy-intensive underground and open-pit operations.

Government and business are also stepping up efforts to address some of the structural challenges holding back investment in the sector. President Cyril Ramaphosa and business leaders have launched Phase 3 of the Government-Business Partnership, with mining identified as one of the key sectors alongside energy and transport logistics.

The partnership has set an ambitious target of securing R50 billion in new capital expenditure commitments from mining companies by February 2028. Another major priority is the rollout of a national digital mining cadastre, which is scheduled for completion by March 2027. The system is intended to tackle the long-standing backlog in prospecting and mining-right applications, improve transparency and make it easier to attract international exploration and investment capital.

The longer-term ambition is even more substantial, with government and industry targeting the unlocking of up to R2 trillion in investment over five years by developing South Africa’s critical mineral resources. The country’s platinum group metals, chrome, manganese and iron ore deposits are expected to play an important role in this strategy as global demand for minerals linked to energy security, infrastructure and new technologies continues to grow.

Logistics remain another crucial part of the mining story. Coal producers such as Thungela Resources have managed to maintain relatively resilient export volumes by making use of third-party rail capacity and taking advantage of gradual improvements in Transnet Freight Rail’s performance. These measures have helped support first-half coal export sales, despite the ongoing challenges facing South Africa’s rail and port infrastructure.

Taken together, these developments point to a mining sector that is becoming more focused on consolidation, energy independence, investment and operational efficiency. While infrastructure constraints, regulatory delays and global commodity-price volatility remain challenges, the combination of renewable power, improved logistics and renewed government-business cooperation could provide a stronger foundation for growth in the years ahead.

The power utility also indicated that it plans to make greater use of surplus generation capacity by exporting electricity to neighbouring markets. This includes efforts to restore electricity supplies to Mozambique’s Mozal aluminium smelter.

In the banking sector, Nedbank received approval from the Central Bank of Kenya for its $842 million, or approximately R13.9 billion, acquisition of NCBA Group. The transaction will give Nedbank a 66% controlling stake in the Kenyan banking group and strengthens its presence elsewhere on the continent.

Shoprite also released its 2026 full-year financial results, reporting continued growth in sales, underlying earnings and dividend distributions, reflecting the retailer’s ongoing resilience in a challenging consumer environment.

Motorists are facing a significant increase in fuel costs from Wednesday, 2 September. The Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources has finalized steep increases, with global oil price volatility and a higher slate levy contributing to the adjustment. The slate levy increased by 21.9 cents per litre to 83.28 cents.

Both grades of petrol will increase by R1.34 per litre, taking the inland price of 95 petrol to R26.92 per litre. Wholesale diesel prices will rise by R2.94 per litre for 0.05% sulphur diesel and R3.15 per litre for 0.005% sulphur diesel, pushing the inland wholesale price of 0.005% diesel above R30 per litre. Illuminating paraffin will increase by R2.13 per litre.

On the policy front, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana has approved the publication of the 2026 annual policy benefit escalations under the Demarcation Regulations, affecting the regulatory framework governing certain insurance and health-related products.

Meanwhile, SASSA old-age grant payments begin on Wednesday, 2 September. Recipients aged 60 to 74 will receive R2,400, while those aged 75 and older will receive R2,420. Treasury is also continuing to focus on an estimated R4.8 billion shortfall in the social grant budget ahead of the October Medium Term Budget Policy Statement.

Overall, Tuesday’s developments point to a mixed picture for the South African economy. While corporate earnings, vehicle sales and Eskom’s financial position provide some positive signals, weak manufacturing activity, falling electricity demand, market volatility and sharply higher fuel prices continue to highlight the pressures facing households, businesses and investors.

title: South Africa’s Key Financial & Macroeconomic Highlights | 2 September 2026
summary: Fuel prices jump sharply as petrol rises R1.34/litre and diesel over 11%, the rand holds near R16.16–R16.19/USD while the JSE slips and gold falls to $4,302.68/oz, the Absa PMI stays in contraction at 45.8, Sibanye-Stillwater's H1 EBITDA doubles to R31.8bn, and eThekwini's municipal debt climbs to around R47bn.
body:
South African motorists are waking up to sharply higher fuel prices from today, adding to concerns about renewed inflationary pressure across the economy. Petrol prices have increased by R1.34 per litre for both 93 and 95 unleaded, taking inland 95 petrol to R26.92 per litre. Diesel prices have climbed even more steeply, rising by between R2.94 and R3.15 per litre, an increase of more than 11%. Inland 50ppm diesel now costs R30.05 per litre. The increases have been driven largely by higher international crude oil prices amid heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, together with adjustments to the slate levy. The Public Servants Association has urged government to reconsider fuel tax levies in an effort to limit the knock-on effects on households and businesses.

In currency markets, the rand remained relatively steady, trading around R16.16 to R16.19 against the US dollar. Broader dollar strength and concerns over rising oil prices continue to weigh on the currency, although domestic market sentiment has provided some support. On the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the All Share Index slipped 0.35%, while the Top 40 Index declined 0.37% as global risk appetite remained subdued. Gold prices also came under pressure, falling to around $4,302.68 an ounce, their lowest level in three weeks, while Brent crude pushed above $95 a barrel as tensions in the Middle East continued to unsettle energy markets.

South Africa’s manufacturing sector remains under pressure. The seasonally adjusted Absa Purchasing Managers’ Index fell to 45.8 in August from 46.8 in July, marking the fourth consecutive month below the 50-point level that separates contraction from expansion. It was also the weakest reading of the year, pointing to continued strain on domestic manufacturing activity and highlighting the broader challenges facing the economy.

The vehicle market, however, provided a more positive signal. NAAMSA reported that new vehicle sales increased by 11.4% year on year in August. While this represents a slight slowdown from the 11.9% growth recorded in July, the industry continues to show signs of resilience despite the broader economic pressures facing consumers and businesses.

In the mining sector, Sibanye-Stillwater reported a strong first half for the period ended June 2026, with adjusted EBITDA doubling to R31.8 billion, supported by stronger precious metals prices. The company’s board has also approved capital deployment towards new gold mining projects in Gauteng and Australia, signalling continued investment despite the challenging operating environment.

Municipal finances remain another area of concern. Debt owed to the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality has climbed to approximately R47 billion, with households accounting for about R35 billion and businesses around R10 billion. The mounting debt highlights the growing financial pressures facing both residents and local government.

Meanwhile, Takealot has revised its free-delivery policy, increasing the minimum order value required for free delivery to R750. The change comes as online retailers continue to adjust their pricing and delivery models in response to rising operating and logistics costs.

title: South African Financial & Economic News Update | 3 September 2026
summary: The rand recovers to around R16.04/USD on softer US data as oil holds near $95 a barrel and gold trades around $4,431/oz; business confidence stays subdued at 38 points, manufacturing contracts for a fourth month, vehicle sales rise 11.4%, and Nedbank/Yellow Door Energy reach financial close on the 49MW Lion Thorn Solar Park.
body:
South African financial markets are navigating a mix of global uncertainty, rising energy costs and cautious domestic business sentiment on Thursday, 3 September 2026.

The rand is trading at around R16.04 to the US dollar, recovering slightly after earlier losses this week. Softer US payroll and manufacturing data have weighed on the dollar, providing some short-term support for emerging-market currencies. The rand is also trading at approximately R21.65 against the pound and R18.60 against the euro. Meanwhile, commodity markets remain firm, with oil prices hovering near $95 a barrel amid continued geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, while spot gold remains elevated at around $4,431 an ounce.

Energy costs continue to be a major concern for the South African economy. September has brought significant fuel price increases, with diesel rising by as much as R3.15 per litre. Nedbank economists expect these higher energy costs to place renewed upward pressure on producer and consumer inflation in the months ahead. This comes despite July producer price inflation easing to 5.7%. Higher diesel prices are also putting additional pressure on logistics and commercial transport operators, although the sector is showing signs of resilience, with sales of extra-heavy commercial vehicles increasing by 24.2% year on year in August.

Business sentiment remains subdued. The RMB/BER Business Confidence Index was broadly unchanged at 38 points in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 39 points in the second quarter. The reading reflects continued caution among South African businesses as high global input costs and weak domestic demand weigh on economic activity. Manufacturing conditions remain particularly challenging, with the Absa Purchasing Managers' Index falling to 45.8 in August, marking the fourth consecutive month of contraction in the sector.

The vehicle market, however, continues to provide a brighter spot. New vehicle sales increased by 11.4% year on year in August, according to NAAMSA, pointing to continued resilience in both consumer and fleet demand despite the broader economic pressures.

Corporate and economic data releases are also in focus today. JSE-listed pharmaceutical group Aspen Pharmacare and healthcare company Discovery Limited are among the companies attracting investor attention. Discovery is releasing its annual results for the financial year ended 30 June 2026, together with its dividend declarations. Statistics South Africa is also scheduled to release its Residential Property Price Index for April 2026 and its report on electricity generated and available for distribution for July 2026.

Eskom's latest financial report has also drawn attention to executive remuneration. Outgoing chief financial officer Calib Cassim received total remuneration of R13.52 million during 2026, exceeding CEO Dan Marokane's reported remuneration of R12.18 million.

In the private sector, Takealot has increased the minimum basket value required for free delivery to R750 as the online retailer adjusts its terms. In the energy sector, Nedbank Corporate and Investment Banking and Yellow Door Energy have reached financial close on the 49 MW Lion Thorn Solar Park. The project has secured power purchase agreements with PPC and private electricity trader POWERX, adding further momentum to South Africa's growing renewable-energy investment pipeline.

Overall, South Africa's economic picture remains mixed. Financial markets are receiving some support from softer US economic data, while strong vehicle sales and continued investment in renewable energy provide positive signals. However, rising fuel costs, persistent manufacturing weakness, subdued business confidence and pressure on household and business budgets continue to pose significant challenges as the country enters the final quarter of 2026.
